final_proof:
Let \(u(t)=\operatorname{Re}f(t)\) and \(v(t)=\operatorname{Im}f(t)\) for \(t\in[a,b]\). Since the real- and imaginary-part maps are continuous, \(u\) and \(v\) are continuous real-valued functions on \([a,b]\). Hence they are Riemann integrable on \([a,c]\), \([c,b]\), and \([a,b]\).

By the definition of the integral of a complex-valued function, for each of \((x,y)=(a,c),(c,b),(a,b)\),
\[
\int_x^y f(t)\,dt=\int_x^y u(t)\,dt+i\int_x^y v(t)\,dt.
\]
Additivity of the real Riemann integral over adjacent intervals gives
\[
\int_a^c u(t)\,dt+\int_c^b u(t)\,dt=\int_a^b u(t)\,dt
\]
and
\[
\int_a^c v(t)\,dt+\int_c^b v(t)\,dt=\int_a^b v(t)\,dt.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_a^c f(t)\,dt+\int_c^b f(t)\,dt
&=\left(\int_a^c u(t)\,dt+\int_c^b u(t)\,dt\right)
+i\left(\int_a^c v(t)\,dt+\int_c^b v(t)\,dt\right)\\
&=\int_a^b u(t)\,dt+i\int_a^b v(t)\,dt\\
&=\int_a^b f(t)\,dt.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(c=a\) or \(c=b\), the same calculation remains valid because the integral over a degenerate interval is zero. Thus the identity holds for every \(c\in[a,b]\).
